comment: Hi Council, Thank you for looking into the affordable housing issue. The zoning restrictions have made it difficult for owners of Single Family zoned homes to provide additional housing. The ADU approvals have been a refreshing change, but unfortunately many people are left out from those strict rules for one reason or another. It seems like the only entities ever allowed to build are these massive conglomerates with big lawyers and lots of money for bribes and fees (though they all look the exact same). I'd like to see individuals who actually live in the community be able to have more control of housing and build structures on their properties. My home is on a large 0.26 lot near Liberty Park. It has a basement apartment that has been grandfathered into approved use. Many of my surrounding neighbors have multi-unit complexes but the whole neighborhood is still zoned as single family. Even though I have ample space to build another structure behind my home for an additional unit, the city has decided I technically already has 2 units. I've tried every angle to attempt to be approved to build on my lot with no success. I've given up at this point. But it is unfortunate since I have the space and resources to provide more housing. The city already turned me down in an attempt to rezone my property as well. • I'd like to see less corporate involvement and less building restrictions for individuals to have condos complexes built. Salt Lake City has so few condo complexes in comparison to apartments. When people own their own units, this prevents rent hikes and people aren't forced to move because the corporate owner decided to raise rent by hundreds of dollars a month. PLEASE APPROVE ONLY CONDO COMPLEXES GOING FORWARD. • Less restrictions on individual homeowners to build additional units on their properties. Let's get creative on types of housing structures allowed as well. It's in backyards, tiny homes, etc. Thank you for reading! Cheers, Becca

I'm sure they'd have no problem meeting that on a yearly basis with all the grants and fundraising they do. That's $4,000-5,000 that could go to road repairs, city employee bonuses, building maintenance, parks and rec maintenance, or towards hiring more fire and police. It's a good example of penny wise and pound foolish. I really think it would be more charitable to the Other Side Academy because after all it's non-profit charity and it's going to help us out a lot with our homeless situation and lead to downtown economic benefits. But I'd like us to do a little better than $1 for a 40 year lease. We can accomplish more good by still being EXTREMELY charitable and generous with pricing but not giving away public land for free. Especially for FOUR decades. For context, 40 years ago Reagan won election for the first time, 40 years ago, the average home was $47,000. 40 years ago there wasn't even personal computers and Apple 2. Microsoft didn't exist. The internet didn't exist. That's an insanely long lease. On a pilot project that may fail in 10 years or less. Just something to think about. I'd appreciate it if it keep it in mind. comment: Dear all, I support the idea of a tiny home village completely. There are a lot of positive impacts for the City in this project. The only negative I saw concerned the assignment of responsibility for remediating the previous landfill to the Other Side Village. I do not believe a community group like TOSV can bear the sole responsibility for cleaning up a city dump we Salt Lakers enjoyed for decades. We should be partners. I need to add that the City's current Remediation methods could be confounded in the eagerness to supply such a needed good to our community on a non-profit's budget. I think the City must partner with TOSV to provide a clean, healthy foot-print on which to build these tiny homes. Engagement with scientists and engineers at the state level, I think, would be a welcome start. The landfill was around long before the EPA regulations of the 1970's were born. The landfill is only a few blocks from the Surplus Canal. My father used to take us kids to watch them dump the trash and burn it on the "wrong" side of town since the founding of our city. I doubt the clean-up will be as straight-forward as the clean-up west of the Gateway plaza. I saw Mayor Becker there, growing his vegetables in boxes above the ground. The soil is still a little contaminated and remediation hasn't completely restored the soil. That's a sad situation but at least there it will take more than a few seasons to clean-up our problem. The tiny homes project is a wonderful idea and a great way to launch opportunities for others to provide homes for our community. The opportunity to fundamentally address issues facing us every day. Bicycle lanes, 20 MPH, Rocky's street flags, you folks at the Salt Lake City government are coming up with some fine ideas on how to handle the population explosion locally. I'm behind you all the way! Bill Komlos,

subject: D7 CIP Application -- Brentwood Circle/Wyoming Street flooding mitigation/D7
comment: Dear Ms. Fowler: Several months ago my neighbor, Jennie McCullough, and I contacted you regarding repeated, significant flooding in our Parleys Way neighborhood. The Mayor's office advised us to apply for a Capital Improvement Project (CIP) to address the problem, and we did, on behalf of ourselves and six other neighbors. We recently heard that the CDOP Board did not send our application forward for consideration, likely because they did not understand the magnitude of the need. However, we also understand that a final decision on funding CIP projects has not yet been made. We are writing today to seek your support for funding the Brentwood Circle and Parleys Way Storm Water Drainage project. Our CIP application included a plan to divert Parleys Way storm water away from Brentwood Circle by installing larger catch basins, replacing transition structures, and enlarging waterways along Parleys Way. In addition, we proposed the installation of a storm water collection line along Wyoming Street. I understand that this part of the proposal was added to Public Utilities' list of rate-payer project requests. In our proposal we asked that the city share in the expense of preventing flooding in our neighborhood. My family has spent $56,000 to recover from flooding and prevent future flooding, and the McCulloughs have spent a similar amount to protect their home from the $10,000-$20,000 in damages and $30,000 each. In addition, the McCulloughs recently had their property re-graded and they installed a concrete barrier and 2-foot in diameter pipe to redirect storm water -- a project that will cost the three homeowners involved an additional $30,000. We are asking for further help from the city's to protect our properties from flooding damage in the future. I'm re-attaching the materials that we submitted for the CIP application; the cover letter explains the project in brief. We would both appreciate the opportunity to schedule a brief, 15-minute meeting with you to discuss the project prior to the City Council's discussion of CIP projects. Please let us know when you might be available. Thanks in advance for supporting our project. Melissa Koerner Jennie McCullough **Jukic responded

subject: Save - I mean, ENJOY Our Foothills
comment: Good Morning, I have been mountain biking the SLC foothills since 1984 when I purchased one of the first mountain bikes in the city. With the development of new trails, infrastructure, and connections between various trail systems over the last 5 years, To me, the trails have combined many elements of outdoor enjoyment, thoughtful design, exhilarating access to natural beauty, and healthy activity. The Wheels and Heels demarcation works well, accommodating hikers, runners, and bikers. Strong work by the Parks people! Last week, I spent an hour at the Avenues Street Fair chatting with a representative from Save Our Foothills, [SOF]. Our exchange was civil and thoughtful. And, I came away with two hour at the Avenue conclusion that two issues SOF are advocating for are misguided. First, they claim there is undeniably anti-new trails. I also noticed that the photographs SOF selected to demonstrate man-made erosion illustrated selective bias. The extreme shots were meant for shock value to encourage petition signing. And the only erosion I've seen was natural after the October 2021 deluge, two slides that actually came from far above, and I covered, a trail. I strongly encourage Phases II and III to continue on schedule. Sincerely Evan Richards Clinical Education Consultant.

subject: Biker/walker commuter safety
comment: Hi City Council, I recently sold my car and have been relying solely on biking, walking, and public transit to get around Salt Lake City. I'm deeply concerned for biker & walker safety on the streets of Salt Lake, as I've found out as a bike commuter our city is designed for cars, not people or bikes. I recently watched this video that showed Salt Lake's streets through the lens of pedestrian and bicyclist safety. Salt Lake City was used as an example of one of the more dangerous places to be a pedestrian and cross the street. This doesn't make me a proud Salt Lake citizen. Our city is designed for cars, and everytime I'm commuting I do fear for my safety here. I would strongly support adding infrastructure to make biking and walking in Salt Lake City safer, including additional protected bike lanes (not just shoulders) across the city, continuous sidewalks, independent traffic lights, and slowing down drivers. This would provide better options for commuters and reduce our dependency on cars, which will also work to improve Salt Lake's air quality (another issue I'm very concerned about, but warrants it's own comment). For being such an active city I'm surprised by the lack of bike infrastructure, and by designing our roads only for cars we discourage commuters from even trying to commute by bike. I would love for Salt Lake to lead the way by following Amsterdam's example, and designing our city for our people and not their cars.
